name: ShareTripwire
one_liner: Self-serve ransomware tripwire for small-business Windows file servers: canary files catch encryption in seconds, cut off the attacking session and guide restore.

buyer.role: IT manager or sole in-house IT generalist (or the owner) at a small business
buyer.company_profile: 10-150 employee firm (architecture, engineering, legal, accounting, manufacturing) with 1-3 on-prem Windows file servers or a NAS-backed share, no SOC and often no EDR on servers; has seen peers hit by ransomware and cannot afford Varonis or Thinkst.

user: The same IT generalist, plus whoever receives the SMS/Teams alert out of hours.

problem.summary: Ransomware typically reaches file servers through one infected PC, encrypts shared folders and deletes shadow copies before anyone notices. File-server behaviour detection is enterprise-priced, deception tools cost thousands per year, and endpoint anti-ransomware on shares blocks legitimate writes like CAD exports. Small firms need cheap, low-false-positive early warning on their shares that tells them which machine is attacking and how to restore.

evidence.claim: A Server 2008 R2 file server was encrypted after ransomware spread from one PC; the malware deleted the shadow copies the admin hoped to restore from.
Admins whose file-server folders were encrypted cannot tell which of several PCs with access was the infected source.
A time-delayed Dharma variant hit a Windows Server 2019 box; the team asks how to detect it earlier.
File-server behaviour detection from Varonis is quote-only and reviewers call it expensive, leaving little for 1-3 server shops.
Endpoint anti-ransomware on file shares produces false positives that block legitimate writes such as AutoCAD exports.
Deception/canary detection is costly for small teams; the median Thinkst Canary deal is about $9,900/year.

why_now.summary: Microsoft's built-in Sysmon on Windows Server 2025 adds free, supported file and process telemetry a tripwire can use to name the attacking process and host, with no third-party driver. Insurers keep asking SMBs for stronger controls before renewal, and canary detection remains priced for larger teams.

features.feature: Windows service that plants hidden, plausibly named canary files and folders across shares and watches them for modify/rename/delete
features.why: Canaries give near-zero false positives compared with entropy or rate heuristics that trip on CAD exports.

features.feature: On trigger: identify the SMB session, user and source host, and optionally close the session and disable the share write (one-click or automatic)
features.why: Directly answers 'which PC is infecting the share' and stops spread.

features.feature: Out-of-band alerts by SMS, email and Teams with plain-language next steps
features.why: The buyer has no SOC; alerts must be actionable by a generalist at 2 a.m.

features.feature: Snapshot guard: scheduled VSS snapshots plus an alert when shadow copies are deleted or vssadmin/wmic shadow commands run
features.why: Shadow-copy deletion is the classic precursor; keeping a restore point is the cheapest recovery.

features.feature: Guided restore checklist that lists affected files by canary timestamps and the last clean snapshot
features.why: Turns panic into a sequence a small team can follow.

out_of_scope: Backup storage (integrates with existing backup instead)
Linux/NAS-native agents in v1 (Windows file servers first)

competitors.name: Thinkst Canary
competitors.how_we_differ: Network-wide deception hardware/software at a ~$9,900/yr median deal; we are file-share-only and priced per server for tiny shops.

competitors.name: Canarytokens (free)
competitors.how_we_differ: Free tokens alert on open but do not watch mass encryption, name the SMB session or block it; we add response and restore.

competitors.name: ManageEngine DataSecurity Plus
competitors.how_we_differ: Full file-server auditing suite from $745/yr for 2 servers that the generalist must configure; we are a 10-minute install focused on one job.

competitors.name: Varonis Data Security Platform
competitors.how_we_differ: Enterprise, quote-only; we target firms Varonis never calls.

competitors.name: Microsoft Defender for Business
competitors.how_we_differ: EDR with automatic attack disruption for SMBs up to 300 users, but servers need an add-on and many small file servers run without it; we add share-level canaries and restore guidance alongside it.

competitors.name: Acronis Cyber Protect
competitors.how_we_differ: Backup-centric anti-ransomware per device; we are detection and session cut-off on the share, usable alongside any backup.

differentiation: One job done for the smallest buyers: canary-based detection on the file share that almost never fires falsely, names the attacking PC, cuts its session and walks a generalist through restore. Cheaper than Thinkst or Varonis, narrower and simpler than ManageEngine, and complementary to whatever backup or EDR they already have.

build.team: 1 technical founder (Windows internals); contractor for a small web dashboard later
hardest_parts: Making canaries attractive to ransomware traversal order yet invisible and harmless to users, indexers and backup software
Safe automatic response: closing SMB sessions without disrupting legitimate users on a false trigger
Earning trust for a small vendor's service running with high privilege on file servers
Out-of-band alerting that still works when the network is under attack

pricing.model: Self-serve per protected file server, monthly or annual, card payment; MSP pricing later
pricing.entry_price: $39/file server/month (or $390/year), first server free for 30 days
pricing.rationale: ManageEngine DataSecurity Plus starts at $745/year for 2 file servers and Thinkst's median deal is about $9,900/year; $390/year per server sits under the generalist's own sign-off limit while covering a solo founder's low running costs.

comparables.price: file server auditing from $745/year for 2 Windows file servers
Standard from $85/year, Advanced from $129/year per device (list)

go_to_market.first_customers: Ten small firms (10-150 staff) with on-prem Windows file servers holding large working files - architecture, engineering, accounting - with one in-house IT person, found via sysadmin communities and IT-generalist forums; a few via the founder's contacts.
go_to_market.channel: Self-serve download with free trial, content marketing (ransomware-on-file-server how-tos ranking for the questions in the evidence), r/sysadmin and Spiceworks community presence; MSP resale later.
go_to_market.wedge: Free 'shadow-copy deletion and canary' check script that tells an admin in 5 minutes whether their file server would notice encryption tonight.

risks: Bundling is high: Defender for Business attack disruption, Synology immutable snapshots and backup vendors' ransomware detection all cover parts of this.
Self-serve SMB acquisition without ad spend is slow; the founder must rely on content and community.
A false-positive session cut-off or a missed detection during a real attack would destroy trust and invite liability claims.
Many small firms are moving files to SharePoint/OneDrive, shrinking the on-prem file-server market.
Ransomware operators may learn to skip or detect canary files.

riskiest_assumption.assumption: Small-business IT generalists will pay $39/server/month for file-share canaries when Defender, backups and free Canarytokens exist.
riskiest_assumption.test: Publish the free check script and a landing page with the price and a 'reserve founder pricing' paid deposit ($39); promote in r/sysadmin, Spiceworks and two IT-generalist newsletters for 2 weeks.
riskiest_assumption.success_signal: At least 500 script downloads and 15 paid deposits within 2 weeks, with at least half from firms of 10-150 employees.

open_questions: How many target firms still run on-prem file servers versus SharePoint?
How often do modern ransomware families touch canary-style files before the bulk of data?
Will MSPs, not end clients, be the real buyer here?
Which insurers accept canary detection as a control?
